title: How DNS finds an address
point: DNS turns a name such as example.com into an IP address by asking a chain of servers, from the root down to the server that holds the name.

overview.name: Why names need DNS
overview.point: Computers connect to each other by IP address while people remember names, so something must turn one into the other.

overview.name: The whole lookup
overview.point: A resolver asks a root server, then a top-level domain server, then the authoritative server, and hands the address back to the browser.

chapters.name: The lookup
chapters.point: One lookup passes through four kinds of servers, and each of them points to the next one until the address is found.

pages.name: Resolver
pages.point: The resolver asks the other servers on behalf of the browser and keeps their answers for later lookups.

sections.name: Cache
sections.point: A resolver answers from its cache for as long as the TTL of the record allows.

sections.name: Recursive queries
sections.point: Without a cached answer, the resolver asks the root, the top-level domain, and the authoritative servers in turn.

pages.name: Root and TLD servers
pages.point: The root servers point to the server of the top-level domain, and that server points to the server that holds the name.

sections.name: Root servers
sections.point: The root servers know where the server of every top-level domain such as `.com` is.

sections.name: TLD servers
sections.point: The server of a top-level domain knows which authoritative server holds each name under it.

pages.name: Authoritative server
pages.point: The authoritative server holds the records of the name and gives the final answer.

sections.name: A and AAAA records
sections.point: An `A` record holds an IPv4 address and an `AAAA` record holds an IPv6 address.

chapters.name: Reference
chapters.point: The terms of this explainer are listed with one sentence each.

pages.name: Terms
pages.point: Each term that the lookup uses is explained in one sentence.

sections.name: TTL
sections.point: TTL is the number of seconds a resolver may keep a record before it asks again.
